title: Towards Understanding the Training of GFlowNets: A Theoretical Perspective

paper.title: Towards Understanding the Training of GFlowNets: A Theoretical Perspective
paper.abstract: Abstract Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn policies that sample discrete objects in proportion to a positive reward. They are trained by minimizing balance objectives, whose exact satisfaction guarantees correct sampling. However, a comprehensive theory linking nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially under evolving sampling distributions and backward policies, is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we develop a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. We first bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss. Then, we show that approximate stationarity controls this distribution error up to a tangent-space residual measuring parameterization incompleteness. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling and fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions, with fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected loss is O ⁡ ( ϵ ¯ 2 + T − 1 ) O(\bar{\epsilon}^{2}+T^{-1}) and expected terminal symmetric KL is O ( ϵ ¯ + T − 1 / 2 ) O(\bar{\epsilon}+T^{-1/2}) under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize the sufficient update decay to approach the residual neighborhood and preserve these rates. These results connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy and clarify how parameterization, coverage, and moving components govern GFlowNet training.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets, Bengio et al. (2021) ; Bengio et al. (2023) ) have emerged as a promising framework for training generative models that sample objects with probabilities proportional to a positive reward. High-reward objects are therefore sampled frequently, while different high-reward regions retain probability mass. This combination of quality and diversity has made GFlowNets useful in various applications such as molecule generation ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Koziarski et al., 2024 ) , combinatorial optimization ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , probabilistic inference ( Manta et al., 2023 ; Deleu et al., 2024 ) , text generation ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and image generation ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Yun et al., 2025 ) . GFlowNets transform the sampling problem into a sequential generation process on a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Starting from an initial state, a forward policy constructs an object through a series of local decisions until it reaches a terminal state. The central idea is to view probability mass as flow through the DAG. If the flow is conserved at intermediate states and the terminal flow matches the reward, then the forward policy samples terminal states from the desired reward-proportional distribution. This global property can be enforced through local or trajectory-level balance conditions, leading to the standard Flow Matching (FM, Bengio et al. 2021 ), Detailed Balance (DB, Bengio et al. 2023 ), and Trajectory Balance (TB, Whitammer et al. 2022 ) objectives. This elegant construction explains what happens when every balance condition is satisfied exactly, but it does not explain what happens during practical training. A parameterized model may attain only a small nonzero loss or approach a stationary point rather than a global minimizer. Moreover, the states, edges, or trajectories used for training may be drawn from an off-policy and time-varying distribution, while the backward policy may be fixed, trained jointly with the balance loss, or updated using a separate criterion. These choices make the objective seen by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) evolve over time. Consequently, to understand GFlowNet training, a systematic study is required to connect loss and stationarity to terminal accuracy while accounting for these moving components. This motivates three essential questions: 1. Does a small balance loss guarantee that the learned terminal distribution is close to the reward-proportional target? 2. When optimization reaches an approximate stationary point, how good is the resulting sampler, and what limits its accuracy? 3. As sampling strategies and backward policies are adapted during training, when can learning still approach the target distribution, and at what rate? Existing studies provide complementary pieces of this picture. Flow-imbalance analyses ( Silva et al., 2025a ) examine how balance violations affect the generated distribution, while generalization analyses ( Krichel et al., 2024 ; Silva et al., 2025b ) study learning from limited observations. Connections to variational inference and entropy-regularized reinforcement learning ( Whitammer et al., 2023 ; Tiapkin et al., 2024 ) , together with advances in loss design ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Fawkes and Hartford, 2026 ) , relate training objectives to distribution discrepancies. However, these relationships do not by themselves connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy. Yu (2025) establishes gradient-convergence results for FM and DB, as well as sample-complexity guarantees for TB. However, the objectives in their analysis differ from the commonly used squared log-ratio loss and do not clarify the quality of parameterized stationary points or the behavior of stochastic training under varying sampling and backward policies. Very recently, Lei et al. (2026) derived total variation guarantees from a uniform residual bound, providing a quantitative measure of sampling accuracy based on balance loss. A comprehensive literature review is available in Appendix A . To answer the above questions, we develop a unified theory for FM, DB, and TB that connects balance loss, stationary-point quality, and finite-time sampling accuracy. Our theoretical results are summarized as follows: 1. Balance loss controls sampling accuracy. For FM, DB, and TB, we bound the terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss, with explicit occupancy-mass and coverage factors. Thus a small loss is informative when the training samples cover the states, edges, or trajectories on which the forward and backward flows disagree. 2. Stationarity implies approximate optimality. We decompose the log-flow imbalance into a gradient-visible tangent component and an orthogonal parameterization residual. This yields an approximate gradient-domination property in which the terminal distribution error is controlled by the gradient norm and a precisely defined parameterization-incompleteness term. Thus, approximate stationarity leads to a nearly accurate sampler. 3. Finite-time convergence with moving training components. We analyze stochastic GFlowNet training when the sampling distribution is fixed or changes in a controlled manner and when the backward policy is fixed, jointly optimized by the balance loss, or updated by a general rule. With fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected balance loss is bounded by O ⁡ ( ϵ ¯ 2 + T − 1 ) O(\bar{\epsilon}^{2}+T^{-1}) , which gives expected terminal symmetric KL of O ( ϵ ¯ + T − 1 / 2 ) O(\bar{\epsilon}+T^{-1/2}) under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize how fast its update must decay to ensure convergence and to preserve these rates. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces FM, DB, and TB in a unified framework. Section 3 relates their expected balance losses to terminal-distribution mismatch. Section 4 establishes the stationarity-to-optimality guarantee, and Section 5 gives the finite-time convergence analysis. Additionally, we extend the analysis to Sub-Trajectory Balance in Appendix E .

4. From Stationarity to Optimality
sections.text: Theorem 3.2 connects distribution error to log-flow imbalance and hence the balance loss. To understand what remains when optimization only reaches a stationary point, we further show that this imbalance can be decomposed into two parts: its projection onto the local tangent space and an orthogonal residual. 5. Convergence Rates of Stochastic GFlowNet Training
sections.text: Section 4 explains when a small gradient implies a small imbalance. We now ask whether stochastic training reaches such a regime, and how quickly. We first fix the sampling distribution, so that tangent geometry directly turns SGD descent into loss contraction. We then allow the sampling distribution to change, and finally allow a separate backward-policy update. The stochastic-optimization, moving-objective, and actor–critic background for is summarized in Appendix A.2 ; detailed proofs and regularity checks appear in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we develop a unified theory that connects balance loss, approximate stationarity, and sampling accuracy for FM, DB, and TB. We bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss and characterize stationary-point quality through a tangent-space residual that vanishes for standard positive tabular models. Under suitable regularity, coverage, and conditioning assumptions, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees and quantify how sampling and backward-policy drift must be controlled to preserve them. Our findings clarify the conditions under which optimization progress leads to accurate reward-proportional sampling, marking a significant advancement in understanding the training of GFlowNets. This insight is valuable for further algorithmic development and real-world applications. Moreover, our analysis builds upon and enhances existing function-approximation and distribution-shift techniques from RL and optimization, indicating their potential applicability to a broader range of fields. However, the guarantees outlined in this paper depend on adequate coverage, well-conditioned effective tangent geometry, and controlled drift. These factors require further verification in practical implementations, particularly when neural networks are involved. We recognize these limitations and view them as important directions for future research, despite the challenges they present.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work and Technical Perspective
sections.text: We review the theoretical development of GFlowNets, emphasizing results on sampling accuracy and learning, and then explain how our analysis connects to techniques in reinforcement learning and optimization.

sections.heading: Foundations and connections to other theories.
sections.text: The foundations of GFlowNets characterize reward-proportional sampling through consistent flows on a construction graph ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Bengio et al., 2023 ) . Flow Matching (FM) and Detailed Balance (DB) impose local consistency, while Trajectory Balance (TB) enforces consistency along complete generation paths ( Whitammer et al., 2022 ) . Under the corresponding support and reward-matching conditions, exact balance yields the target terminal distribution. Sub-Trajectory Balance (SubTB) interpolates between edge and complete-trajectory constraints, providing intermediate scopes for credit assignment ( Madan et al., 2023 ) . Appendix E extends our analysis to SubTB under its stated conditions. These results establish the correctness of balanced solutions; understanding an imperfectly trained, parameterized sampler requires additional analysis. Connections to other inference and learning frameworks clarify these objectives. Whitammer et al. (2023) establish expected-gradient identities between balance objectives and variational inference under specified trajectory distributions and choices of the differentiated parameter block. Tiapkin et al. (2024) reformulate GFlowNet learning as entropy-regularized RL using a particular reward and regularizer structure. More recently, Deleu et al. (2025) identify an equivalence between Relative Trajectory Balance and the KL-regularized RL method Trust-PCL. Loss-design theory further connects regression penalties to distributional objectives: Hu et al. (2025) relate expected regression gradients to gradients of divergences between flows on minimal cuts under an appropriate sampling structure. Fawkes and Hartford (2026) develop an f f -trajectory-balance family with corresponding on-policy f f -divergence gradients and target-preserving off-policy minima under their conditions. Such identities illuminate optimization signals and loss design, but require further arguments to characterize parameterized stationary points or finite-time sampling accuracy.

sections.heading: Imbalance sensitivity and representational limits.
sections.text: Silva et al. (2025a) investigate how balance violations affect sampling accuracy. Their Theorem 1 bounds terminal total variation (TV) for a specified perturbation of an initially balanced network, obtained by adding and propagating flow. The bounds reveal dependence on the flow scale and target mass of downstream terminal states. This is a sensitivity result for the stated perturbation construction, rather than a general bound on arbitrary expected training loss. They also characterize expressiveness limitations of GFlowNets using 1-WL graph neural networks, propose more expressive look-ahead policies, and introduce flow consistency in subgraphs (FCS) as a distributional diagnostic with theoretical connections to TV. Their representational results concern which distributions a model class can express. Our tangent residual instead measures imbalance unexplained by local parameter derivatives at the current model.

sections.heading: Generalization, coverage, and statistical guarantees.
sections.text: Krichel et al. (2024) formalize generalization and reward-perturbation stability and empirically study generalization to longer trajectories. Their stability proposition assumes globally minimized TB, a fixed uniform backward policy, and reward functions with equal total mass; the length-generalization experiments do not establish an unrestricted extrapolation guarantee. Silva et al. (2025b) develop data-dependent PAC-Bayesian bounds using bounded FCS risk, together with oracle bounds for terminal KL and DB-based risk under their sampling and regularity assumptions. Their Proposition 4.2 also bounds terminal TV through an expected squared trajectory log-density ratio and a distribution-mismatch factor involving χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence. Its expectation samples terminal states from a chosen distribution and then backward trajectories; the ratio uses normalized target probabilities. Our training measure can instead weight states, edges, or complete trajectories, with normalization terms eliminated by symmetrization. Thus, coverage-dependent links between average discrepancy and sampling error already exist. Their analysis motivates Subgraph Asynchronous Learning, which divides training across smaller subnetworks. Our contribution is a common occupancy-discrepancy analysis for FM, DB, and TB, and its connection to stationary-point quality and stochastic optimization. The population bounds here complement statistical generalization guarantees: coverage alone does not justify substituting empirical loss for population loss.

sections.heading: Comparison with Lei et al. (2026) .
sections.text: Lei et al. study loss sensitivity, showing that small terminal TV need not prevent large balance loss, and develop guarantees in the converse direction. Their Theorem 3.5 bounds TV by 1 − e − 2 ​ c 1-e^{-2c} when every squared TB residual is at most c 2 c^{2} ; the corresponding FM/DB bound is 1 − e − 2 ​ L ​ c 1-e^{-2Lc} for maximum trajectory length L L . Their Theorem 3.6 provides a probabilistic certificate using independent forward trajectories and backward trajectories initialized from the target distribution. Its global form requires target-terminal samples; restricted-target sampling yields a subgraph certificate. They also propose adaptive reference flows to stabilize training, analyzing the associated fidelity trade-off. Relative to Lei et al., our distributional statement uses expected squared log-ratio loss under a general, possibly off-policy training measure and controls terminal symmetric KL through occupancy mass and coverage. It does not require their uniform pointwise residual condition, but it can be vacuous under poor coverage and is a population inequality rather than a finite-sample certificate. The two analyses therefore control different error metrics under different hypotheses; neither gives an unconditional tightness ordering.

sections.heading: Extensions of the underlying environment.
sections.text: Other theoretical work broadens the modeling setting. Lahlou et al. (2023) formulate generalized GFlowNets using measurable spaces, flow measures, and Markov kernels, extending balance conditions and sampling correctness to continuous and hybrid spaces under assumptions including finite absorption. Morozov et al. (2025) revisit discrete non-acyclic environments, clarifying flow definitions, the role of backward policies, and the relationship between total flow and expected trajectory length. They also analyze fixed-backward training and stability issues when the backward policy is learned. These extensions address structural questions beyond the discrete DAG setting used here; transferring our approximate-balance and optimization analysis to them requires revisiting the occupancy and trajectory assumptions.

sections.heading: Compatible approximation, natural gradients, and approximate PL geometry.
sections.text: Compatible function approximation regresses advantages onto policy-score features, connecting least-squares coefficients to natural policy gradients (NPG) ( Sutton et al., 1999 ; Kakade, 2001 ) . For general policy classes, transferred approximation error evaluates this regression under a comparator policy’s occupancy, making distribution shift part of the optimality analysis ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . Under Fisher nondegeneracy and bounded transferred error, Liu et al. (2020) analyze NPG through compatible regression and a comparator-policy KL potential. For momentum policy gradient, Ding et al. (2022) derive a bound on the optimality gap by an approximation floor plus a multiple of the gradient norm. Related analyses develop this route for stochastic policy gradients ( Fatkhullin et al., 2023 ) and NPG with Hessian-aided momentum variance reduction ( Feng et al., 2024 ) . In the context of GFlowNets, the regression target is log-flow imbalance and the features are its parameter derivatives. The residual is local to the tangent space and measured under the training distribution, unlike transferred advantage error under a comparator occupancy. The feature Gram matrix is the Gauss–Newton matrix of the squared-imbalance loss with the training measure fixed, and need not be a policy Fisher. Raykov and Veiga (2026) use the forward trajectory Fisher to precondition GFlowNet balance-loss gradients. This Fisher coincides with the imbalance Gram matrix for the forward-only TB block under on-policy weighting with backward policy and source flow held fixed; their decomposition and approximation guarantees concern update geometry rather than approximation-dependent gradient domination. A lower bound on the nonzero Gram eigenvalues turns the projection identity into an approximate PL inequality: squared gradient norm controls loss above the tangent-residual floor. This also connects to nonlinear least-squares and tangent-kernel analyses ( Karimi et al., 2016 ; Jacot et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Stochastic-gradient baselines and objective drift.
sections.text: The fixed-sampling part of Section 5 belongs to the classical stochastic-approximation lineage initiated by Robbins and Monro ( Robbins and Monro, 1951 ) and developed for recursive algorithms and stochastic optimization in later treatments ( Bottou et al., 2018 ) . Conditional unbiasedness and a second-moment bound for the balance-gradient oracle, together with smoothness, give the usual expected-descent recursion. In our setting, the effective Fisher lower bound and the tangent residual turn this recursion into an approximate Polyak–Lojasiewicz inequality: the loss contracts until it reaches the parameterization residual floor, with an O ⁡ ( T − 1 ) O(T^{-1}) loss rate under harmonic stepsizes. The terminal-distribution bound then takes a square root, giving the O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) rate in Corollary 5.6 . This is a population result for the stated training measure, rather than a generic claim that every nonconvex SGD trajectory converges globally. When the sampling law changes with the iterate, or the backward policy is updated seperately, the objective seen by the SGD oracle thus evolves during training. Two-time-scale stochastic approximation provides the classical limiting-ODE and finite-time perspectives for coupled updates ( Borkar, 1997 ; Konda and Tsitsiklis, 2004 ; Kaledin et al., 2020 ) . The controlled-gradient and controlled-sampling assumptions in Section 5.2 and Section 5.3 make the first- and second-moment effects of this drift explicit. This interpretation is related to small-gain analyses of single-timescale actor–critic methods ( Olshevsky and Gharesifard, 2023 ; Chen and Zhao, 2023 ) and to finite-time analyses with an evolving reward or objective ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , but the constants here are defined for the GFlowNet sampling measure and its imbalance features.

They are trained by minimizing balance objectives, whose exact satisfaction guarantees correct sampling. However, a comprehensive theory linking nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially under evolving sampling distributions and backward policies, is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we develop a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. We first bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss. Then, we show that approximate stationarity controls this distribution error up to a tangent-space residual measuring parameterization incompleteness. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling and fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions, with fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected loss is O ⁡ ( ϵ ¯ 2 + T − 1 ) O( ar{\epsilon}^{2}+T^{-1}) and expected terminal symmetric KL is O ( ϵ ¯ + T − 1 / 2 ) O( ar{\epsilon}+T^{-1/2}) under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize the sufficient update decay to approach the residual neighborhood and preserve these rates. These results connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy and clarify how parameterization, coverage, and moving components govern GFlowNet training. 1. Introduction Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets, Bengio et al. (2021) ; Bengio et al. (2023) ) have emerged as a promising framework for training generative models that sample objects with probabilities proportional to a positive reward. High-reward objects are therefore sampled frequently, while different high-reward regions retain probability mass. This combination of quality and diversity has made GFlowNets useful in various applications such as molecule generation ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Koziarski et al., 2024 ) , combinatorial optimization ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , probabilistic inference ( Manta et al., 2023 ; Deleu et al., 2024 ) , text generation ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and image generation ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Yun et al., 2025 ) . GFlowNets transform the sampling problem into a sequential generation process on a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Starting from an initial state, a forward policy constructs an object through a series of local decisions until it reaches a terminal state. The central idea is to view probability mass as flow through the DAG. If the flow is conserved at intermediate states and the terminal flow matches the reward, then the forward policy samples terminal states from the desired reward-proportional distribution. This global property can be enforced through local or trajectory-level balance conditions, leading to the standard Flow Matching (FM, Bengio et al. 2021 ), Detailed Balance (DB, Bengio et al. 2023 ), and Trajectory Balance (TB, Whitammer et al. 2022 ) objectives. This elegant construction explains what happens when every balance condition is satisfied exactly, but it does not explain what happens during practical training. A parameterized model may attain only a small nonzero loss or approach a stationary point rather than a global minimizer. Moreover, the states, edges, or trajectories used for training may be drawn from an off-policy and time-varying distribution, while the backward policy may be fixed, trained jointly with the balance loss, or updated using a separate criterion. These choices make the objective seen by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) evolve over time. Consequently, to understand GFlowNet training, a systematic study is required to connect loss and stationarity to terminal accuracy while accounting for these moving components. This motivates three essential questions: 1. Does a small balance loss guarantee that the learned terminal distribution is close to the reward-proportional target? 2. When optimization reaches an approximate stationary point, how good is the resulting sampler, and what limits its accuracy? 3. As sampling strategies and backward policies are adapted during training, when can learning still approach the target distribution, and at what rate? Existing studies provide complementary pieces of this picture. Flow-imbalance analyses ( Silva et al., 2025a ) examine how balance violations affect the generated distribution, while generalization analyses ( Krichel et al., 2024 ; Silva et al., 2025b ) study learning from limited observations. Connections to variational inference and entropy-regularized reinforcement learning ( Whitammer et al., 2023 ; Tiapkin et al., 2024 ) , together with advances in loss design ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Fawkes and Hartford, 2026 ) , relate training objectives to distribution discrepancies. However, these relationships do not by themselves connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy. Yu (2025) establishes gradient-convergence results for FM and DB, as well as sample-complexity guarantees for TB. However, the objectives in their analysis differ from the commonly used squared log-ratio loss and do not clarify the quality of parameterized stationary points or the behavior of stochastic training under varying sampling and backward policies. Very recently, Lei et al. (2026) derived total variation guarantees from a uniform residual bound, providing a quantitative measure of sampling accuracy based on balance loss. A comprehensive literature review is available in Appendix A . To answer the above questions, we develop a unified theory for FM, DB, and TB that connects balance loss, stationary-point quality, and finite-time sampling accuracy. Our theoretical results are summarized as follows: 1. Balance loss controls sampling accuracy. For FM, DB, and TB, we bound the terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss, with explicit occupancy-mass and coverage factors. Thus a small loss is informative when the training samples cover the states, edges, or trajectories on which the forward and backward flows disagree. 2. Stationarity implies approximate optimality. We decompose the log-flow imbalance into a gradient-visible tangent component and an orthogonal parameterization residual. This yields an approximate gradient-domination property in which the terminal distribution error is controlled by the gradient norm and a precisely defined parameterization-incompleteness term. Thus, approximate stationarity leads to a nearly accurate sampler. 3. Finite-time convergence with moving training components. We analyze stochastic GFlowNet training when the sampling distribution is fixed or changes in a controlled manner and when the backward policy is fixed, jointly optimized by the balance loss, or updated by a general rule. With fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected balance loss is bounded by O ⁡ ( ϵ ¯ 2 + T − 1 ) O( ar{\epsilon}^{2}+T^{-1}) , which gives expected terminal symmetric KL of O ( ϵ ¯ + T − 1 / 2 ) O( ar{\epsilon}+T^{-1/2}) under uniform coverage.
